design_detail: Population-based cohort of 49,321 Swedish men conscripted for military service in 1969–70 at age 18 to 20. Cannabis, tobacco and alcohol use were self-reported once, at conscription, in non-anonymous questionnaires; lung cancer was taken from national registers by record linkage (inpatient Patient Register to the end of 2009, Cause-of-Death Register to the end of 2006). Cox regression of time to lung cancer by lifetime cannabis use (ever against never; never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times), crude, tobacco-adjusted and fully adjusted. Exposure was recorded before the outcome, but the study is a historical record-linkage analysis of data collected for conscription.
can_establish: Whether men who reported more cannabis use by age 18 to 20 were diagnosed with lung cancer more often over the next 40 years than men who reported none, after adjustment for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory illness and occupation as recorded at that time.
cannot_establish: That smoking cannabis causes lung cancer, or the risk in men who never smoked tobacco (too few to analyse), in women, above about age 60 or with later patterns of use and products: use after conscription, how cannabis was smoked, how much and whether tobacco was mixed in were never recorded, and the number of cancers in each cannabis group is not given in the text or tables.

sample.recruitment: Registry/conscription: all men conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–70 (born 1949–51), which the authors say covered more than 97% of Swedish men of that age, 2–3% being excused for disqualifying mental or physical conditions (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men conscripted in 1969–70 at age 18 to 20. The models are complete-case analyses: men without cannabis answers (3,768 for ever use, 3,800 for frequency) or with other missing predictors were left out, and 10 of the 189 lung cancers were excluded for missing predictor information.
sample.demographics: Men only, aged 18 to 20 at baseline. At conscription 41.4% did not smoke tobacco, 11.2% smoked 1–5 cigarettes a day, 20.7% 6–10, 23.1% 11–20 and 3.6% more than 20; 10.5% had ever used cannabis and 1.7% more than 50 times; physician-diagnosed respiratory conditions about 2% in every cannabis group; occupation from the 1970 census, about half manual skilled or unskilled (Table 1).
sample.attrition: During follow-up 2,958 men (6.0%) died of causes other than lung cancer and 930 (1.9%) emigrated, both censored; 44,257 to 44,285 men entered the adjusted models (about 90% of the cohort).
sample.selection_effects: Population-based and nearly complete for Swedish men of that age, so selection into the cohort is not the concern. Limits to generalising: men only, Swedish cannabis and tobacco use of 1969–70, and follow-up ending at about age 60. The men who did not answer the cannabis questions (about 7.6%) had a lower lung cancer risk than men who reported never using cannabis (fully adjusted HR 0.41, 0.17 to 0.99), so non-responders differed in some way the paper does not explain.

exposure.measurement: Non-anonymous self-report at conscription: ever against never use of cannabis, and lifetime frequency in six bands (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50, more than 50 times); the bands follow an earlier analysis of the same cohort, and this paper calls more than 50 times 'heavy' use. No biological verification; the authors cite a validation study of self-reported drug use in this cohort as showing reasonable accuracy.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime number of uses by age 18 to 20 only. No quantity, potency, duration, method of smoking (joint or pipe) or tobacco mixed in, and no measure of cannabis use at any time after conscription over the 40 years; smoking is assumed as the route.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco (cigarettes a day at conscription, five answers collapsed into three bands: none, 1–10, more than 10) and alcohol (grams a week from five questions, four levels) were adjusted for, each measured once. Of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 756 (91.0%) also smoked tobacco and 514 (61.8%) more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 54.7% and 23.2% of the men who reported never using cannabis (editors' arithmetic from Table 1). Other drug use was collected at conscription but not used in the analysis. Whether tobacco was mixed into cannabis is unknown.

comparison.controls: Men who reported never using cannabis at conscription (40,397; 44.8% did not smoke tobacco, 31.5% smoked 1–10 cigarettes a day and 23.2% more than 10).
comparison.matching: None. Cox models adjusted for tobacco (three bands), alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) and socioeconomic status (occupation in the 1970 census).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tobacco and cannabis use after conscription; how much tobacco was smoked within the coarse bands (the top band runs from 11 to more than 20 a day); occupational and environmental exposures, diet and family history of lung cancer; use of other drugs. None was adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; 54.7% of the men who reported never using cannabis smoked tobacco (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Lung cancer coded ICD-8/9 162 or ICD-10 C33–C34 in any diagnostic position in the Swedish Patient Register (inpatient care) from conscription to the end of 2009, or as the underlying cause in the National Cause-of-Death Register to the end of 2006; emigration from the Total Population Register. The Swedish Cancer Register was not used.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite 78% to 99% concordance between lung cancer records in the Patient Register and the Cause-of-Death or Cancer Registers, and sensitivities of about 80% to 95% for administrative lung cancer codes in studies elsewhere. Of the 189 cases, 95 were in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only and 6 in the death register only.
outcomes.operationalization: Time to a first lung cancer record, censored at death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009; person-time from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men who died in 1969), about 1.9 million person-years per line of analysis. Proportional hazards checked with log survival plots.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: one outcome, but ever use and five frequency bands were each tested in three models, with p < 0.05 as the threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes came from national registers, independent of the conscription questionnaire.

analysis.effect_sizes: Hazard ratios with 95% CIs (Tables 2–4). Lifetime frequency against never (crude; tobacco-adjusted; fully adjusted): once 2.07 (1.06–4.06); 1.48 (0.75–2.91); 1.52 (0.77–3.01). 2–4 times 0.95 (0.39–2.33); 0.65 (0.26–1.58); 0.66 (0.27–1.62). 5–10 times 1.02 (0.32–3.20); 0.66 (0.21–2.09); 0.68 (0.21–2.16). 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26–5.74); 1.68 (0.78–3.62); 1.68 (0.77–3.66). More than 50 times 3.72 (1.96–7.06); 2.24 (1.17–4.29); 2.12 (1.08–4.14). Ever against never: 1.90 (1.30–2.75); 1.25 (0.85–1.83); 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco against none, fully adjusted: 1–10 a day 2.34 (1.47–3.70), more than 10 a day 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Missing cannabis answers against never, fully adjusted: 0.41 (0.17–0.99) and 0.40 (0.16–0.98). No absolute risks by group are given; editors' calculation of the base rate: 189 of 49,321 men (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) had a lung cancer record by the end of 2009, about 9 per 100,000 person-years in the analysed cohort (179 cases over about 1.9 million person-years).
analysis.covariates: Tobacco (three bands), alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions at conscription and socioeconomic status (occupation, 1970 census), all measured once at baseline.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The frequency bands, including 'more than 50 times', follow an earlier analysis of the same cohort (Zammit et al., 2002, cited for consistency); the label heavy is this paper's.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports only the more-than-50 band, the one band significant after adjustment, and omits the null ever-use result after tobacco adjustment, the lack of a gradient across bands and the crude and tobacco-only estimates (all in the Results and tables). Tobacco-stratified analyses are in Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, described as unstable or inestimable; the supplement was not available to this reader.
analysis.power: 179 cases in the models; the number among the 831 men in the heaviest band is not given in the text or tables (Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year, was not extracted); too few men used cannabis without tobacco for stratified analyses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Men who reported more than 50 lifetime uses at age 18 to 20 had about twice the hazard of a lung cancer record by about age 60 (fully adjusted 2.12, 1.08 to 4.14), with an interval reaching close to 1; the estimate fell from 3.72 unadjusted to 2.24 with a three-band tobacco adjustment, ever use was not associated after tobacco adjustment (1.25, 0.84 to 1.87), and the lower bands showed no gradient. Of the heaviest band 91% also smoked tobacco, and no estimate could be made for men who did not.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports 'more than a twofold risk' for heavy use 'even after statistical adjustment for baseline tobacco use' and concludes that the study provides 'initial longitudinal evidence that cannabis use might elevate the risk of lung cancer' (p. 1 of the online-first PDF); the conclusion adds that the finding requires further replication (p. 8). The Discussion proposes that the findings be integrated into drug-prevention programmes as initial evidence of the risks of marijuana smoking for lung cancer (p. 7), and argues that unmeasured changes in use after conscription would bias the estimate toward the null (p. 8). Gaps: the label 'heavy' for more than 50 lifetime uses by age 20; an abstract silent on the null ever-use result, the missing gradient and the near-1 lower limit; and a one-sided bias argument, since later tobacco smoking, more common in men who used cannabis, could bias the estimate away from the null, which the authors cover only as residual confounding by tobacco. The conclusion itself is hedged ('might', 'requiring further replication') and the limitations are stated candidly.

timeline.event: Sidney et al.: Kaiser Permanente cohort in California, no association between cannabis smoking and lung cancer; this paper notes its members were followed only to a mean age of 42 (as cited).
Hashibe et al.: population-based case-control study in Los Angeles, no association (as cited).
This cohort: HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription, no gradient below that band, no association for ever use after tobacco adjustment.

Zhang et al.: pooled analysis of six case-control studies in the International Lung Cancer Consortium, habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (0.66–1.38), known here only through the National Academies committee's account.

National Academies committee: 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and lung cancer, naming this cohort as a study outside the pooled analysis that points to an increased risk.
Muheriwa-Matemba et al., systematic review by route: the reviews it included did not conclusively link cannabis smoking and lung cancer.

replication.where_it_stands: The only cohort with follow-up of decades among the sources read. Its raised estimate in the heaviest band stands against the null pooled case-control analysis and has not been repeated in another cohort in the sources read; it rests on one baseline report of cannabis and tobacco use, with 91% tobacco co-use in that band, and on follow-up that ends before the ages at which most lung cancers are diagnosed.

funding.funder: Supported indirectly by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (salary support for R. C. Callaghan), and by a research grant from the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research (FAS 2009-1611 to P. Allebeck; salary support for A. Sidorchuk). The paper states that the funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, manuscript preparation or approval to publish, and that the views are not necessarily the Ministry's.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Northern British Columbia, University of Toronto and CAMH (Callaghan); Karolinska Institutet (Allebeck, Sidorchuk); North-Western State Medical University, Saint Petersburg (Sidorchuk). No cannabis- or tobacco-industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort, or pooled cohorts, that records cannabis and tobacco use repeatedly through adult life (including how cannabis is smoked, how much and whether tobacco is mixed in), includes enough people who smoke cannabis but never tobacco, follows them with cancer-register outcomes into the ages at which most lung cancers occur, and reports absolute risks by group.

domains.note: Tobacco, the main confounder, was measured once at age 18 to 20 in three coarse bands; 91% of the heaviest cannabis band smoked tobacco and 61.8% more than 10 a day, against 23.2% of the never group. Adjustment for these bands alone cut the ever-use estimate from 1.90 to 1.25 and the heaviest band from 3.72 to 2.24, so residual confounding by tobacco amount within bands and by smoking after conscription is plausible and would run away from the null. Occupational exposures, diet, family history and other drugs were not adjusted for, and estimates among men who did not smoke tobacco could not be made.

A single non-anonymous self-report of lifetime frequency at age 18 to 20 stands for 40 years of exposure: no use after conscription, no method, amount, potency or tobacco mixing. The authors expect under-reporting from non-anonymity and report anecdotal over-reporting to avoid military training; with several bands and a confounded exposure, the direction of the resulting bias is not certain.
Population-based cohort covering more than 97% of Swedish men of that age, followed through national registers from baseline; only 1.9% emigrated.
No intervention after exposure is described that would differ by cannabis use.

About 7.6% lacked cannabis answers and 10 of 189 cancers were dropped for missing predictors (complete-case analysis). The men without cannabis answers had a lower lung cancer risk than the never group (fully adjusted 0.41, 0.17 to 0.99), so missingness was related to the outcome; the effect on the heavy-against-never contrast is unclear.

Register-based lung cancer records, independent of the exposure report; cited concordance between registers 78% to 99%. Inpatient and death records rather than the cancer register, and death records only to 2006, may miss some cases, but not in a way linked to cannabis answers given decades earlier.

No registered protocol; the frequency bands were taken from an earlier paper on this cohort, which limits the choice of cut-off, but ever use and five bands were each tested in three models without correction, and the abstract reports only the one significant band.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because confounding by tobacco and the single baseline measure of exposure could each change the estimate materially, and the remaining tobacco confounding most plausibly biases away from the null. The design's strengths are real: a near-complete national cohort, outcomes from registers and 40 years of follow-up. The study may be cited for the adjusted association between reporting more than 50 lifetime cannabis uses at age 18 to 20 and a lung cancer record by about age 60, with its crude and tobacco-adjusted versions, the null ever-use result and the absent gradient; not for an effect of smoking cannabis, for people who never smoked tobacco, for women, for later or current patterns of use and products, or for risk at older ages.

key_findings.finding: 49,321 men aged 18 to 20 conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–1970 (more than 97% of Swedish men of that age; 2–3% were excused for disqualifying conditions), linked to the Patient Register, the National Cause-of-Death Register and the Total Population Register.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Materials and methods › Data sources; Swedish male conscripts' files

key_findings.finding: Cannabis use was self-reported once, at conscription, in a non-anonymous questionnaire: ever against never, and lifetime frequency (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times); the bands follow an earlier analysis of the cohort, and this paper labels more than 50 times heavy use. 10.5% (5,156) reported lifetime use and 1.7% (831) more than 50 uses.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Materials and methods › Measurement of cannabis use

key_findings.finding: Tobacco was measured once, at conscription, by cigarettes smoked a day (none 41.4%, 1–5 11.2%, 6–10 20.7%, 11–20 23.1%, more than 20 3.6%), collapsed into three bands for the models: none, 1–10 and more than 10 a day. Confounders adjusted: tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) and socioeconomic status from occupation in the 1970 census.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Measurement of tobacco use; Potential confounders

key_findings.finding: Table 1: of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 60 (7.2%) did not smoke tobacco, 242 (29.1%) smoked 1–10 a day, 514 (61.8%) more than 10 and 15 (1.8%) had no tobacco answer; of the 40,397 men reporting never using cannabis, 18,100 (44.8%) did not smoke tobacco, 12,725 (31.5%) smoked 1–10 a day and 9,364 (23.2%) more than 10. Alcohol above 250 g a week: 192 (23.1%) against 918 (2.3%). Respiratory conditions: 18 (2.2%) against 747 (1.9%). The Results say about 91% of the heaviest band reported some tobacco use.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (never and more-than-50 columns)
key_findings.note: 756 of 831 is 91.0% (92.6% of the 816 with a tobacco answer); editors' arithmetic.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men) to lung cancer, death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009, about 1.9 million person-years in each line of analysis. Lung cancer (ICD-8/9 162; ICD-10 C33–C34) came from the Patient Register in any diagnostic position to the end of 2009 and from the Cause-of-Death Register as underlying cause to the end of 2006; cited concordance between registers 78% to 99%, and sensitivity of administrative codes about 80% to 95% elsewhere.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Study outcome; Validity of lung cancer outcome codes; Statistical analyses

key_findings.finding: 189 incident lung cancers (95 in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only, 6 in the death register only); 2,958 men (6.0%) died of other causes and 930 (1.9%) emigrated; ten cases were excluded for missing predictor information, leaving 179 in the analyses. Cases by cannabis group are shown only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Tables 2-4 (n = 179 in the titles)
key_findings.note: Figure 1's values were not extracted, so no absolute risk by cannabis group is given; editors' calculation of the base rate: 189 of 49,321 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) by the end of 2009.

key_findings.finding: More than 50 lifetime uses against never (Table 4, 44,257 men, 179 cancers): crude HR 3.72 (95% CI 1.96 to 7.06), tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17 to 4.29), fully adjusted 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), described by the authors as more than a twofold risk even after adjustment for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (more than 50 times row; footnotes a and b)

key_findings.finding: Ever against never use (Table 3, 44,285 men, 179 cancers): crude 1.90 (1.30 to 2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85 to 1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84 to 1.87); the authors say tobacco adjustment greatly attenuated the risk and further adjustment did not change it.

Lower frequency bands, fully adjusted against never: once 1.52 (0.77 to 3.01), 2–4 times 0.66 (0.27 to 1.62), 5–10 times 0.68 (0.21 to 2.16), 11–50 times 1.68 (0.77 to 3.66); crude, once 2.07 (1.06 to 4.06) and 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26 to 5.74). The authors state that the results did not show a clear dose–response relationship.

Tobacco against none, with cannabis and the other covariates in the model: 1–10 cigarettes a day 2.34 (1.48 to 3.71) and more than 10 a day 5.06 (3.25 to 7.86) with ever use; 2.34 (1.47 to 3.70) and 5.03 (3.23 to 7.81) with cannabis frequency; crude 2.29 (1.48 to 3.57) and 5.16 (3.45 to 7.73). The authors call this a strong dose–response relation.

Men without cannabis answers (3,768 on ever use, 7.64%; 3,800 on frequency, 7.70%) were not more likely to develop lung cancer than men reporting never using cannabis: ever-use item crude 0.52 (0.24 to 1.10), tobacco-adjusted 0.47 (0.21 to 1.07), fully adjusted 0.41 (0.17 to 0.99); frequency item 0.51 (0.24 to 1.09), 0.47 (0.21 to 1.06), 0.40 (0.16 to 0.98).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Missing data; Results, 5th paragraph and its continuation after Table 4

key_findings.finding: Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) did not give compelling results: there were too few people who used cannabis but not tobacco and too few lung cancers, even when men smoking 5 or fewer cigarettes a day were grouped with those who did not smoke.

Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on use before conscription and none on tobacco or cannabis use after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the men in the heavy band also reported tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have inflated their use to be exempted from military training. They argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null.
The authors note that the only earlier cohort ended at a mean age of 42 and that the median age at a first lung cancer diagnosis is about 70; their cohort was followed for 40 years from age 18 to 20.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: men born in 1949 to 1951 were 58 to 60 at the end of 2009.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the authors call their primary finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise the risk of lung cancer; the Discussion proposes that the findings be used in drug-prevention programmes.

Funding as printed: an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (salary support for the first author) and a research grant from the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research (FAS 2009-1611; salary support for the third author); the funders had no role in the study or the decision to publish. No conflicts of interest declared.

reporting_issues.issue: Heavy use is defined as more than 50 lifetime uses in the Methods, Results and Table 4, but as at least 50 uses in the first paragraph of the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysis uses the more-than-50 band (Table 4), which is the definition to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives n = 44,284 for the Cox analyses that produced HR 2.12, but Table 3 (ever use) gives 44,285 and Tables 2 and 4 (frequency, the source of 2.12) give 44,257.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 44,257 with the heavy-use estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say approximately 91% and the Discussion more than 91% of the heaviest band reported tobacco use; Table 1 gives 756 of 831 (91.0%), or 92.6% of the 816 with a tobacco answer (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; about 91% is the figure to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of lung cancers in each cannabis group is given only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year, and not in the text or tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: No absolute risk can be stated for the heavy-use group from the text or tables; only the cohort's overall base rate (189 of 49,321) is available.

verification.source_read: PDF, online-first version (published online 12 July 2013) without printed page numbers, 10 pages (/mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Cannabis/Callaghan_2013_LungCancerCohort.pdf); text extracted once with pdftotext -layout: all text, Tables 1 to 4 with footnotes, the Figure 1 legend (the stacked bar chart, viewed on a rendered page, was not extracted), acknowledgments (funding), conflict statement and reference list. The electronic supplementary material (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2) was not available and was not read. The printed article (reference record) is pp. 1811–1820; page references here are to the PDF's own pages 1 to 10.
